items.title: Introducing Quine: An AI research system designed for the complexity of biology
items.summary:
Biology doesn't operate in silos, and neither should the AI representation of it. Quine is an early-stage research effort to create a multimodal world model of biology. By connecting insights across biological scales and modalities, Quine helps scientists computationally search a space far larger than intuition allows and prioritize hypotheses before they reach the lab. Experimental results provide important feedback, helping researchers sharpen future research directions.

The post Introducing Quine: An AI research system designed for the complexity of biology appeared first on Microsoft Research.

items.content: At a glance Harnessed Agentic RL: Microsoft Research Asia introduces a training paradigm in which the same agent harness used in deployment participates directly in reinforcement learning, removing the need to reimplement the agent inside the training framework. Lightweight by design: Agent Lightning v1.0 delivers a complete agent RL control plane in roughly 3,500 lines of code. Native Kubernetes support: agents run as standard Kubernetes jobs on self-managed clusters, cloud Kubernetes, or local infrastructure, with no dependency on paid commercial sandbox services. Data-efficient training recipe: an end-to-end coding agent pipeline raised Qwen3.5-9B from 41.8% to 56.4% Pass@1 on SWE-bench Verified, a 14.6 percentage point gain, using only about 6,000 training samples based on open sourced dataset. AI agents have evolved from single models to complex full-stack systems built from models, tools, and execution environments. Their capabilities increasingly depend on the agent harness that coordinates them from outside the model. Reinforcement learning (RL) is an approach where AI systems learn through trial and error, guided by rewards and penalties for their actions. RL can make those agents better, but most agent RL systems require developers to reimplement the agent inside the training framework. That is costly, and it means the agent being trained is not quite the agent that gets deployed. To address this, researchers at Microsoft Research Asia have introduced the Harnessed Agentic RL training paradigm and open-sourced a fully rebuilt Agent Lightning v1.0 (opens in new tab) . Compared with the original, Agent Lightning, v1.0 puts more emphasis on staying lightweight, on integrating with real harnesses, and on a complete, reproducible agent RL training pipeline. Agent Lightning v1.0 was rebuilt around Harnessed Agentic RL, with key improvements: Lightweight : the entire framework is about 3,500 lines of code. Agent Lightning v1.0 implements a complete Harnessed Agentic RL system in a codebase that is small and clear enough to understand, modify, and extend. Training on a real agent harness : agents reach the model through the large language model (LLM) proxy in Agent Lightning v1.0, leaving existing harness code unchanged. Native Kubernetes support : agents run directly as Kubernetes jobs, without external commercial sandbox services. Self-managed clusters and local infrastructure alike can support rollouts at scale. A complete coding agent training example : an end-to-end pipeline built on Qwen3.5-9B raised Pass@1 on SWE-bench Verified from 41.8% to 56.4%, an absolute gain of 14.6 percentage points, using only about 6,000 training samples. The limits of traditional agentic RL Traditional agentic RL assumes the training framework owns the interaction loop with the environment. In a ReAct-style loop, the model generates an action, the environment returns an observation, the observation is appended to the context, and the model generates the next action, so the whole rollout maps onto one continuous token trajectory. Early RL systems such as verl, AReaL, and slime were built this way, which meant training an agent required rebuilding its loop inside the RL framework. Real harnesses have outgrown that assumption. Coding agents such as mini-SWE-agent, OpenHands, OpenCode, Claude Code, and Codex each bring their own context management, tool protocols, execution logic, and dependencies, as do general-purpose agent systems. Rebuilding one for training is expensive, and the rebuilt agent may no longer behave in the same way as the deployed agent. Agent Lightning takes a different route. It places an LLM proxy between the agent and the model. The agent continues to run as before: simply point the endpoint that previously called the model API at Agent Lightning, and the training framework can observe and record its model calls. In v1.0, the researchers go further and formally define this paradigm as Harnessed Agentic RL: whichever agent harness is used in deployment is the harness that takes part directly in reinforcement learning during training (Figure 1). Figure 1. Traditional agentic RL compared with Harnessed Agentic RL. In traditional agentic RL, the training framework manages the environment and the agent loop. In Harnessed Agentic RL, the harness manages both. Four challenges in training with real harnesses A core difference between Harnessed Agentic RL and traditional agentic RL is that the environment interaction loop is handled by the agent harness rather than the training framework. The training system can only observe a series of LLM request and response pairs, so a single rollout may be split into a variable number of training samples. This brings four key challenges: Retokenization and sample merging : Harnesses keep context as text, but RL training needs the token IDs sampled during the rollout. Passing text through the chat template and tokenizer again can shift token boundaries, so adjacent calls cannot always be merged into one sample. Advantage calculation : Retokenization, subagents and context summarization can split one rollout into several samples. Computing baselines and advantages directly at the sample level causes rollouts that produce more samples to be counted repeatedly, which alters the original statistical relationships at the rollout level. Loss normalization : Averaging loss by sample count gives more weight to rollouts that produce more samples. Since sample count is often just a product of harness behavior, loss normalization must also avoid being distorted by it. Training backend scheduling : Sample count and length are known only after the harness finishes, while GPU counts and data/tensor parallel configurations are usually fixed. The backend has to map a variable workload into fixed resources. Spotlight: Event Series Microsoft Research Forum Join us for a continuous exchange of ideas about research in the era of general AI. Watch the latest episodes on demand. Watch on-demand Opens in a new tab Building a complete agent RL control plane in 3,500 lines of code In system design, Agent Lightning v1.0 treats simplicity as its first principle. The entire framework is about 3,500 lines of code, with three core components: the API Gateway, the Rollout Controller, and the Customized Trainer (Figure 2). The API gateway stores rollouts, models, and events, and serves as an OpenAI-compatible LLM proxy. It links every model call from the harness to its rollout and records the prompts, responses, and log probabilities that training needs. The rollout controller starts and manages agent execution, either as local processes or as standard Kubernetes jobs, keeping agent execution separate from the trainer. The customized trainer, built on verl, creates rollouts, waits for them to finish, collects samples, and assembles the final training samples through a sample adapter. As a result, for an existing agent harness, simply pointing the model endpoint at the Agent Lightning proxy is usually enough to connect quickly to RL training. Figure 2. The Agent Lightning v1.0 system architecture showing the API gateway, rollout controller, and customized trainer. Collocated async RL Rollout times vary widely across agents. Synchronous RL waits for the slowest agent in a batch and leaves GPUs idle, while fully asynchronous RL raises utilization but needs separate GPU pools for rollout and training. In response, Agent Lightning v1.0 introduces Collocated Async RL, which lets rollout and model updates share the same set of GPUs. Once the system has collected enough rollouts, the update begins: the API Gateway pauses accepting new requests and waits for requests already in progress to finish, and rollout resumes after the update completes. The entire state transition is transparent to the external agent harness. In experiments, this approach achieved about a 2x end-to-end speedup over synchronous RL while using fewer GPUs than conventional asynchronous RL (Figure 3). Figure 3. Synchronous RL, asynchronous RL, and Collocated Async RL compared. Collocated Async RL raises utilization while occupying fewer GPUs. Running agents on Kubernetes Collecting enough rollouts means running many agents at once, which consumes substantial CPU, memory, and compute resources. Other Harnessed Agentic RL frameworks often host those agents on commercial sandbox services such as Modal Sandbox or E2B, where cost climbs quickly with scale. Instead, Agent Lightning v1.0 runs them as standard Kubernetes jobs, reusing existing self-managed clusters, cloud Kubernetes, or local infrastructure (Figure 4). Existing compute resources are used more efficiently, large rollouts cost less, and the whole pipeline stays open source and reproducible. Figure 4. The Rollout Controller in Agent Lightning v1.0 provides native Kubernetes support, running agents directly as standard Kubernetes jobs. 6,000 training samples, a 14.6-point performance gain To test the approach, researchers built a full pipeline on SWE-smith, mini-SWE-agent, and Qwen3.5-9B, covering data cleaning, environment construction, reward-hacking safeguards, and RL training. The training set holds about 6,000 samples and needs no large-scale compute. RL training alone raised Qwen3.5-9B from 41.8% to 56.4% on SWE-bench Verified, a gain of 14.6 percentage points. The coding agent experiments further confirm the earlier analysis of two challenges: advantage calculation and loss normalization. Compared with sample-level handling, rollout-level advantage combined with rollout-level normalization achieves a higher validation reward and keeps policy entropy more stable during training (Figure 5). Figure 5. Pass rate and policy entropy for Qwen3.5-9B on the SWE-smith validation set. items.content: At a glance A new form of computing . Zero-knowledge proofs let you run a workload and receive, alongside the result, a short proof that the program ran correctly. Anyone can check the proof in milliseconds, without rerunning the program, without trusting whoever ran it, and without needing data on which the program was run. Three grand challenges have stood in the way of broad adoption : making proofs fast enough to produce, making them available to normal programs without cryptographic expertise, and resting them on cryptography that will still be trusted many decades from now. Magnetar makes major progress on all three challenges. It proves programs written in Rust, Go, or C, runs 10 to 39 times faster on average than the prior fastest comparable systems, and rests its security only on standard hash functions. It is the latest result of more than a decade of research at Microsoft Research on making zero-knowledge proofs practical. A new form of computing Every result a computer produces comes with an implicit question: did the program run as claimed and produce correct outputs? Today, answering that question often requires a degree of trust alongside verification. We trust the operator, the vendor, the counterparty, or the agent, and we rely on contracts, audits, and logs to establish that trust. Zero-knowledge proofs offer a fundamentally different approach to establishing trust. A program runs, and along with its output it produces a short proof, a cryptographic certificate that this program, on these inputs, produced this output. The proof is small and fast to check. Whoever receives it can confirm the result in milliseconds without rerunning the program, and can pass the proof on to anyone else who needs the same assurance. With the zero-knowledge property, the proof also reveals nothing about inputs that should stay private. This changes what correctness means in the real world. A result no longer has to be trusted because of who produced it. It can be checked because of what accompanies it. An AI agent acting on someone’s behalf could attach a proof that each action complied with the policy it was given. Regulated financial institutions could prove that transactions were processed correctly without making their transactions public. These become possible once producing a proof is as routine as running the program. Three grand challenges Zero-knowledge proofs were invented in the 1980s, and the ideas behind proving program execution have been around nearly as long. What has kept them from becoming a general tool is three challenges that have resisted being solved at the same time. Efficiency . Producing a proof has historically taken millions of times more computation than running the program itself. Years of research have brought that overhead down, but the fastest systems have achieved their speed by making compromises elsewhere. Generality and usability. Many proof systems require developers to manually rewrite their program as a cryptographic circuit, which is a fixed arithmetic description of that exact computation. This takes months. Every change to the application means a new circuit, and the translation is itself a frequent source of security bugs. A general-purpose alternative is to prove the execution of an ordinary processor, so that any compiled program can be proven as written. Until recently, that generality came at a steep cost in speed or security. Security. A proof is only as strong as the cryptography beneath it. Many proof systems rest on elliptic curves, which can be broken by a sufficiently powerful quantum computer. Microsoft is addressing this problem with its Quantum Safe Program, which will move its products and services to post-quantum cryptography, a goal it recently accelerated to 2029 . Post-quantum proof systems already exist, but some rest on lattice assumptions, and most rest on new cryptographic functions invented to reduce the cost of proving. These new cryptographic functions have not faced the decades of scrutiny given to the cryptography protecting today’s internet, and some rest on mathematical conjectures about error-correcting codes that have not been proven. They have bought their speed with strong assumptions. Spotlight: Event Series Microsoft Research Forum Join us for a continuous exchange of ideas about research in the era of general AI. Watch the latest episodes on demand. Watch on-demand Opens in a new tab More than a decade of work For more than a decade, Microsoft Research has worked on making zero-knowledge proofs and verifiable computing practical. Early research followed two approaches, both practical only for small programs. The first (opens in new tab) (opens in new tab) lets a verifier check a long computation through a short conversation with the prover using a technique called the sum-check protocol (opens in new tab) , but this applied only to computations with a particular layered structure. The second (opens in new tab) (opens in new tab) used elliptic-curve cryptography to create very small proofs for almost any computation. But this requires a one-time trusted setup involving secret information which, if leaked, could allow anyone to forge proofs. This approach is also vulnerable to quantum computers. In 2019, a new zero-knowledge proof system called Spartan returned to the sum-check approach and made it work for general-purpose programs without a trusted setup. Spartan can also be instantiated with different cryptographic building blocks. That flexibility is what later allowed the proof system to be built on hash functions alone. A sequence of results then filled in the remaining pieces: Phalanx (opens in new tab) , in 2021, showed how to exploit repetition, such as a processor running the same instruction cycle on every step, to prove computations an order of magnitude faster than Spartan. Magnetar’s processor description is built on this idea. Nova (opens in new tab) , HyperNova (opens in new tab) , NeutronNova (opens in new tab) , Neo and SuperNeo (opens in new tab) showed that stopping Spartan’s proving early, and folding the partial results together, makes it practical to prove computations of any size at far lower cost. Brakedown (opens in new tab) , in 2021, introduced a fast hash-based commitment scheme and combined it with Spartan, giving the first Spartan variant whose security rests on standard hash functions. Spice (opens in new tab) , Lasso (opens in new tab) , Nebula (opens in new tab) , and then Twist and Shout (opens in new tab) made the memory operations at the heart of a general-purpose processor inexpensive to prove, and Jolt (opens in new tab) showed that combining them with Spartan can efficiently prove the execution of a complete processor. Earlier this year, Vega (opens in new tab) applied this line of work to digital identity, proving facts from a government credential in under a tenth of a second . More recently, BinarySpartan (opens in new tab) brought Spartan to binary fields, where a processor’s logic and standard hash functions can be efficiently expressed. BinarySpartan also relies on Ligerito (opens in new tab) , a Brakedown-style commitment scheme with much shorter proofs, and on ring switching (opens in new tab) , which makes it efficient to commit to vectors of bits. Each of these solved a piece of the problem. Magnetar is where the pieces come together. Magnetar Magnetar is a zero-knowledge virtual machine, or zkVM, and it makes major progress on all three challenges at once. Figure 1. Magnetar proves a program’s execution and returns a small proof that anyone can check, with security resting only on standard hash functions. It is general-purpose. Magnetar proves the execution of RISC-V, an open processor architecture with mature compilers for every mainstream language. A developer writes a program in Rust, Go, or C, compiles it as usual, and Magnetar proves it as written. Consider what this means in practice. A business policy, a data pipeline, or an interpreter for the Ethereum Virtual Machine (EVM) is just a program, and the engineers who already maintain it can prove their executions exactly as written. As a result, proving stops being a specialist activity. It is faster than prior systems in the same class. Magnetar proves 7.2 to 8.7 million processor instructions per second on a laptop. Across 15 benchmark programs, from cryptographic hashing to token transfers inside a small EVM interpreter, it is 10 to 39 times faster on average than the fastest existing zkVMs on the same machine, and more than 300 times faster than two others on a token-transfer benchmark. An optimized Magnetar proves 9.5–12.8 million cycles per second, which increases each speedup reported here by about 1.3×. Its proofs verify in about 12 milliseconds. Its security rests on standard cryptography. Magnetar depends on a standard hash function such as SHA-256 or SHA-3, the same primitives that already protect every organization’s systems. It requires no elliptic curves, no lattices, no special-purpose hash functions, no trusted setup, and no unproven conjecture about error-correcting codes. Hash functions are the most thoroughly studied primitives in the cryptographic toolkit, and they are the basis of the stateless hash-based signatures that NIST standardized as its own conservative post-quantum option. For a system that must still be trustworthy in many decades to come, relying only on standard hash functions removes a cryptographic migration from the roadmap. The same design decision pays a second dividend. Checking a Magnetar proof consists mostly of evaluating standard hash functions and binary-field arithmetic, which are exactly the operations Magnetar proves efficiently. Verifying a proof is therefore an ordinary workload for it. This is what allows Magnetar to prove computations of any size, by proving them in pieces and then combining the pieces. This also allows Magnetar to prove a long-running system such as a ledger or a blockchain. The technical paper gives the full design, security analysis, and measurements. Looking ahead Magnetar advances zero-knowledge proofs and verifiable computing to a stage where they can be built on the cryptography that organizations already trust, at speeds that make it usable, by engineers who write normal code. Magnetar enables a future where cryptographic proofs are a routine output of computation. We expect that technology leaders will stop asking whether proofs of execution are practical and focus instead on which results would they prefer to verify rather than taking on trust . If you’re interested in exploring how zero-knowledge proofs can support your use case, we’d love to hear from you (opens in new tab) . items.content: Microsoft researcher and collaborator combine new mathematical ideas with human-directed AI to resolve a central problem in high-dimensional geometry and probability At a glance Fundamental scientific breakthrough: Researchers resolved the Kannan-Lovász-Simonovits (KLS) conjecture, a 31-year-old problem widely regarded as one of the central open questions in high-dimensional geometry, with implications for statistics, optimization, algorithms, and computer science. A universal geometric principle: The result establishes a universal geometric principle for log-concave distributions, showing that simple flat cuts can capture their narrowest bottlenecks within a fixed factor, regardless of dimension. Human-AI collaboration: The breakthrough emerged from a human-directed agentic research process in which AI systems explored mathematical possibilities while researchers evaluated, pruned, and redirected the search. Independent confirmation: Multiple independent researchers have validated this research, identifying its central criterion as the key breakthrough, followed by a machine-checked formal verification. For decades, a fundamental question about the difficulty of computing in high-dimensional spaces has resisted proof. New research resolves this question, removing a major theoretical obstacle to understanding the efficiency of randomized algorithms used across science and computing. The Kannan–Lovász–Simonovits (KLS) conjecture was proposed in 1995. It asks whether, for a broad class of high-dimensional probability distributions, the best flat or hyperplane cut is always nearly as effective as the best cut of any shape. More precisely, KLS predicts that the two differ by no more than a universal constant, regardless of the number of dimensions. This would establish a dimension-free geometric principle with important consequences for high-dimensional geometry, probability, and theoretical computer science. Because the geometry of these cuts governs how quickly random walks can explore a distribution, KLS also plays a central role in the theory of high-dimensional sampling. Figure 1: An illustration of the KLS Conjecture (simplified) on regular tetrahedron. Since 1995, mathematicians have accumulated evidence that the conjecture was true, but a complete proof remained elusive. Now, two researchers, including Xinzhi Zhang from the Machine Learning and Optimization group at Microsoft Research, have proved the KLS conjecture (opens in new tab) . They have shown that the relationship holds with a fixed bound, regardless of how many dimensions a shape has. Before this work, the best known result (opens in new tab) , established in July 2026, allowed that bound to grow slowly as the number of dimensions increased. This work establishes a fundamental geometric principle: high-dimensional spaces are better behaved than previously known, and the obstacles to navigating them do not grow without bound as dimensions increase. PODCAST SERIES The Shape of Things to Come Join Microsoft’s Doug Burger and guests as they dig into the fundamental truths about AI and how it will reshape the future. Listen now Opens in a new tab The importance of the KLS conjecture was recognized across the field long before it was resolved. In its 2017-18 Annual Report, the Mathematical Sciences Research Institute (MSRI) (opens in new tab) called it “a central open problem in high-dimensional convex geometry.” The Simons Institute (opens in new tab) described it as “one of the most important open problems in convex geometry.” In the proceedings of the 2022 International Congress of Mathematicians (ICM) (opens in new tab) , Ronen Eldan noted its broad implications for high-dimensional convex and computational geometry. Quanta Magazine (opens in new tab) wrote that KLS “lies at the heart of many questions in statistics and computer science.” Technical details The authors began by improving the July 2026 result in order to make the mathematical bound more precise. Working with AI agents in a structured, human-directed process, they explored more than 100 candidate approaches, many involving lengthy calculations with higher-order tensors. This produced a new mathematical criterion that became the foundation of the final proof. The authors then discovered that the new criterion could be applied recursively. Each improved bound could be fed back into the same argument to produce a still tighter one. In the October 1, 2026 version of the paper, this reduced the dependence on dimension to the iterated logarithm. This function grows extraordinarily slowly, but it still grows with the dimension and therefore did not yet fully resolve the conjecture. The final step was to repeat the entire recursive refinement, rather than applying it only once. This idea was inspired by the authors’ earlier work on fast algorithms for linear programming. The authors proved that the small errors introduced at each stage shrink fast enough that their total remains bounded by a universal constant, independent of the dimension. This eliminated the dependence on the number of dimensions and completed the proof in the October 4, 2026 version of the paper. The recursive method, its repeated application, and the proof that the accumulated errors remain bounded are original contributions of the researchers. AI tools helped explore candidate approaches, carry out detailed derivations, prepare the manuscript, and perform internal proof checks. The researchers determined the mathematical direction, selected the promising ideas, assembled them into the final argument, and verified the proof. Independent confirmation On the same day that the authors posted their complete proof, a separate group of leading experts posted a full proof (opens in new tab) that they developed in parallel. Their work built upon the findings in the first version (opens in new tab) of the Microsoft paper, calling it “the crucial step in the proof.” A third proof (opens in new tab) which appeared separately on the same day relies on a closely related idea. In addition, a Lean 4 formalization (opens in new tab) was subsequently released, combining the key criterion from the first Microsoft paper with additional research. Independent proofs are among mathematics’ strongest forms of validation because they demonstrate that a result does not rest on a single chain of reasoning. The subsequent appearance of alternative approaches and formal verification further strengthens confidence that the field has uncovered a genuine underlying principle rather than a fragile technical argument. The authors have also shortened their proof and verified the streamlined argument in Lean; they plan to release both after final review. Together, these developments provide complementary forms of confirmation. Human-AI guidance In the process of proving KLS, this research also demonstrates the power of having researchers direct AI rather than simply asking AI to solve a complex problem through a single end-to-end run of a frontier model or agent. The authors used an agentic search process with iterative, human-assisted “pruning”: As multiple agents explored variations of an idea in parallel, the researcher examined their intermediate result, eliminated unpromising directions, and passed the most promising result to the next round. Roughly one hundred research trajectories were explored before the key breakthrough emerged. In a separate track of the project, the authors made repeated unguided attempts to solve the same problem with several leading AI models, using roughly the same total token budget as the main process. That effort fell short of the goal. The eventual success depended on both the capabilities of the AI systems and the mathematical judgment of the researchers. Conclusion Taken together, resolving KLS settles a central problem in high-dimensional geometry. A wide range of results that previously relied on the conjecture as an assumption can now be stated unconditionally. The proof therefore provides a stronger foundation for research in convex geometry, probability, and theoretical computer science. The work also demonstrates how carefully guided human-AI collaboration can contribute to genuine scientific discovery while reinforcing, rather than replacing human insight. It highlights the continuing importance of scientific judgment in identifying promising directions, recognizing conceptual connections, and seeing when a partial insight points toward a deeper result. The authors are now simplifying the proof and extending its formal verification so that the mathematics and theoretical computer science communities can more easily examine the result and build on it. Acknowledgements Thank you to our co-author Zhao Song for his contributions to this work, and Victor Reis (opens in new tab) and Ishai Menache for helpful discussions throughout the project. The authors proved that the small errors introduced at each stage shrink fast enough that their total remains bounded by a universal constant, independent of the dimension. This eliminated the dependence on the number of dimensions and completed the proof in the October 4, 2026 version of the paper. The recursive method, its repeated application, and the proof that the accumulated errors remain bounded are original contributions of the researchers. AI tools helped explore candidate approaches, carry out detailed derivations, prepare the manuscript, and perform internal proof checks. The researchers determined the mathematical direction, selected the promising ideas, assembled them into the final argument, and verified the proof. Independent confirmation On the same day that the authors posted their complete proof, a separate group of leading experts posted a full proof (opens in new tab) that they developed in parallel. Their work built upon the findings in the first version (opens in new tab) of the Microsoft paper, calling it “the crucial step in the proof.” A third proof (opens in new tab) which appeared separately on the same day relies on a closely related idea. In addition, a Lean 4 formalization (opens in new tab) was subsequently released, combining the key criterion from the first Microsoft paper with additional research. Independent proofs are among mathematics’ strongest forms of validation because they demonstrate that a result does not rest on a single chain of reasoning. The subsequent appearance of alternative approaches and formal verification further strengthens confidence that the field has uncovered a genuine underlying principle rather than a fragile technical argument. The authors have also shortened their proof and verified the streamlined argument in Lean; they plan to release both after final review. Together, these developments provide complementary forms of confirmation. Human-AI guidance In the process of proving KLS, this research also demonstrates the power of having researchers direct AI rather than simply asking AI to solve a complex problem through a single end-to-end run of a frontier model or agent. The authors used an agentic search process with iterative, human-assisted “pruning”: As multiple agents explored variations of an idea in parallel, the researcher examined their intermediate result, eliminated unpromising directions, and passed the most promising result to the next round. Roughly one hundred research trajectories were explored before the key breakthrough emerged. In a separate track of the project, the authors made repeated unguided attempts to solve the same problem with several leading AI models, using roughly the same total token budget as the main process. That effort fell short of the goal. The eventual success depended on both the capabilities of the AI systems and the mathematical judgment of the researchers. Conclusion Taken together, resolving KLS settles a central problem in high-dimensional geometry. A wide range of results that previously relied on the conjecture as an assumption can now be stated unconditionally. The proof therefore provides a stronger foundation for research in convex geometry, probability, and theoretical computer science. The work also demonstrates how carefully guided human-AI collaboration can contribute to genuine scientific discovery while reinforcing, rather than replacing human insight. It highlights the continuing importance of scientific judgment in identifying promising directions, recognizing conceptual connections, and seeing when a partial insight points toward a deeper result. The authors are now simplifying the proof and extending its formal verification so that the mathematics and theoretical computer science communities can more easily examine the result and build on it. Acknowledgements Thank you to our co-author Zhao Song for his contributions to this work, and Victor Reis (opens in new tab) and Ishai Menache for helpful discussions throughout the project. items.title: Scaling NVIDIA TensorRT Performance Optimization Beyond a Single Build Route with the Global Performance Tuner, Part 1
items.summary: Edge Computing Scaling NVIDIA TensorRT Performance Optimization Beyond a Single Build Route with the Global Performance Tuner, Part 1 Oct 23, 2026 By Jian Hu and Lin Chai Like Discuss (0) L T F R E AI-Generated Summary NVIDIA TensorRT builds inference engines by making interdependent scheduling decisions across graph transformations, fusion, implementation selection, memory placement, and quantization. A mathematical framework models compilation as a builder algorithm generating candidate solutions and a searching algorithm selecting the fastest feasible one under accuracy constraints. The Global Performance Tuner, released in TensorRT 11.1 , introduces customizable build routes that expand the solution space and validate each candidate against end-to-end accuracy and performance. Three principles guide the tuner: accuracy-aware tuning, customizable build routes, and a large solution space from which the fastest acceptable engine is selected. Next Steps Read the Global Performance Tune
items.content: Edge Computing Scaling NVIDIA TensorRT Performance Optimization Beyond a Single Build Route with the Global Performance Tuner, Part 1 Oct 23, 2026 By Jian Hu and Lin Chai Like Discuss (0) L T F R E AI-Generated Summary NVIDIA TensorRT builds inference engines by making interdependent scheduling decisions across graph transformations, fusion, implementation selection, memory placement, and quantization. A mathematical framework models compilation as a builder algorithm generating candidate solutions and a searching algorithm selecting the fastest feasible one under accuracy constraints. The Global Performance Tuner, released in TensorRT 11.1 , introduces customizable build routes that expand the solution space and validate each candidate against end-to-end accuracy and performance. Three principles guide the tuner: accuracy-aware tuning, customizable build routes, and a large solution space from which the fastest acceptable engine is selected. Next Steps Read the Global Performance Tuner documentation to understand the feature and its configuration options. Read Part 2 of this series for the algorithm and architecture design plus best practices. Powered by NVIDIA Nemotron. AI-generated content may summarize information incompletely. Verify important information. Learn more Deploying a trained neural network involves more than translating each operator into a GPU kernel. It is a compilation problem with many legitimate answers. For example, when NVIDIA TensorRT builds an engine, it makes interdependent decisions about graph-IR transformations, fusion, implementation selection, memory placement, and quantization. This process is called scheduling. Different scheduling choices can preserve model semantics yet produce very different inference performance, making scheduling central to deep learning compiler optimization. No single scheduling strategy is best for every model and deployment environment. A transformation that accelerates one network may slow another. A kernel that is faster in isolation may interact poorly with fusion, tensor layouts, or memory traffic elsewhere in the graph. Aggressive scheduling may improve performance while violating an application’s accuracy requirement. These coupled, model-dependent effects often appear only after the complete engine is built and measured, making the right strategy increasingly difficult to predict. This post is Part 1 of a two-part series that is intended to develop a clearer way of reasoning about performance optimization. It explores questions such as: What makes one compiled engine better than another? Why can individually promising decisions fail end to end? How should accuracy constrain performance optimization? It introduces the Global Performance Tuner , a feature for automatic performance tuning released in TensorRT 11.1 , and explores these questions through an intuitive example and mathematical framework. What challenge does the Global Performance Tuner feature solve? The following analogy illustrates the motivation for building the Global Performance Tuner feature in TensorRT. Imagine a chef with one excellent dish that has pleased three regular customers for years. One likes spice, another sweet-and-sour flavors, and the third extra salt. The chef combines chili, syrup, lemon, and salt in one standard recipe that satisfies all three. One day, a new fourth customer arrives who dislikes spice. Keeping the chili disappoints the newcomer; removing it risks losing the first customer. The root cause of the chef’s dilemma is the method of adding the seasonings does not scale out: the number of interacting exceptions grows with the customer base, and a change for one customer can degrade the meal for another. Figure 1. One fixed recipe does not scale to conflicting customer preferences A scalable approach keeps the base dish but makes the seasonings configurable. The chef records an appropriate combination for each regular customer. For a new customer with unknown preferences, the chef offers free samples with different combinations, rejects unsuitable variations, and keeps the one the customer likes best. Figure 2. Customize the flavor for each customer Mapping this analogy to deep learning compilation, TensorRT is the chef, its shared pipeline the base recipe, tunable compiler configurations the seasonings, and the compiled engine the finished dish. Each ONNX model is a customer. Performance tuning offers samples, and end-to-end performance reflects customer satisfaction. Historically, TensorRT performance optimization has started with internal KPI models. Engineers study these workloads, identify optimizable patterns, and encode their findings as heuristics in the TensorRT default scheduling strategy. Each heuristic captures expert knowledge and allows users to benefit automatically from optimizations discovered on representative models. As models and deployment environments diversify, this approach leads to a scaling problem similar to the one described in the analogy. A heuristic inspired by one internal KPI model joins the shared strategy and may help familiar patterns while causing a regression for an unseen external model. Adding another check or exception may protect that model, but repeating the process makes the scheduling logic increasingly difficult to extend. The problem appears in three related forms: H euristic sprawl: Each new model-specific heuristic introduces another rule whose interactions with existing rules must be understood and maintained. As these rules accumulate, the code becomes unmaintainable, and improvements for one family of models can unintentionally affect another. Performance-accuracy entanglement: Reduced-precision kernels and other aggressive optimizations can improve performance while introducing numerical differences that exceed an application’s acceptable tolerance. Higher-precision choices may reduce that risk but sacrifice performance. Performance and numerical acceptability therefore cannot always be optimized independently. Performance customization: Scheduling choices that work well for one model or GPU may not work well for another. Encoding every successful choice into one universal scheduling strategy makes it difficult to specialize TensorRT efficiently for a continually expanding range of external models, hardware platforms, and application requirements. Tuning provides a scalable complement to heuristic optimization. Mathematical theory for deep learning compiler performance This section develops an abstract mathematical model of deep learning compiler performance. The purpose is to separate two fundamental questions: What executables a compiler can construct for a model How the compiler selects one from those possibilities for optimal performance Concept: Model, model space Let \(m\) represent a model and \(M\) represent the collection of all models under consideration, called the model space: \(m \in M\) Here, a model is an abstract description of the computation to be compiled. Its concrete representation may be an ONNX graph, a network created through the TensorRT API, a PyTorch model, or another frontend representation that fully specifies the model computation. Concept: Solution, solution space Given a model \(m\) as input, a deep learning compiler constructs an executable output for the target hardware, defined as a solution. The same model can generally be compiled into different solutions under different scheduling policies. Let \(s\) represent one such solution, and let \(S\) represent the collection of possible solutions, called the solution space. s ∈ S = { s 0 , s 1 , s 2 , . . . , s n } s \in S = \{s_0, s_1, s_2, …, s_n\} A solution is an abstraction of executable computation on the target hardware. Concretely, a solution may be a TensorRT engine or a cubin of serialized sequence of GPU kernels. More abstractly, it may also be a compiler’s intermediate representation (IR), provided that the representation uniquely determines the final executable under the remaining compilation process. Each solution also defines a function from the model’s input domain to its output codomain: \(s : X \rightarrow Y\) \(s(x) = y\) Here, \((x,y)\) is an input-output pair for the sequence of GPU kernels that implements the neural network. At this level of abstraction, the model describes the intended computation, while a solution describes one particular way of realizing that computation on the target hardware. Principle of determinism Statement: When both a deterministic program and its complete execution environment remain fixed, the program has a fixed underlying run time. This principle serves as a modeling assumption for performance analysis. Under a rigorous interpretation, the environment includes the input data, target device, software stack, GPU frequency, temperature, power state, system load, and other execution conditions that may influence runtime. In practice, not every environmental variable can be controlled perfectly, so repeated runtime measurements exhibit noise. If this disturbance is modeled as independent Gaussian noise, the average of repeated measurements is the maximum-likelihood estimation of the underlying mean run time. Once the execution environment has been fixed at the level required by the abstraction, each solution can be associated with one characteristic runtime. This association enables runtime to be represented as a mathematical function. Concept: Run time function The run time function \(T\) maps each solution to its runtime on a specified target device under a fixed execution environment: T : S → ℝ + T : S \rightarrow \mathbb{R}^+ \(T(s_0) = t_0\) The environment is treated as fixed and is therefore omitted from the notation. Concept: Builder algorithm A builder algorithm (also called a performance scheduler) is a mapping from the model space to the power set of solution space. When given a specific model as input, the builder algorithm will output a solution space with a given accuracy requirement. B : M → 2 S B: M \rightarrow 2^S B ( m ) = { s 1 , s 2 , . . . , s n | max x ∈ X ⁡ ‖ s ( x ) − y ‖ ≤ ϵ } = S B(m) = \{s_1, s_2, …, s_n \mid \max_{x \in X} \norm{ s(x) – y } \leq \epsilon \} = S In the accuracy condition shown above, the input–output pairs \((x, y)\) are treated as reference values, and \(ε\) represents the accuracy tolerance threshold. The reference data, comparison metric, and tolerance are treated as fixed context and are therefore suppressed from the arguments of \(B\). Ideally, the builder algorithm should generate a sufficiently rich set of solutions to contain \(s^*\), the optimal solution: the fastest feasible solution in the modeled solution space. s ∗ ∈ B ( m ) s^* \in B(m) Concept: Searching algorithm A searching algorithm (also called a solver of solution space) is a mapping from the power set of solution space to the solution space. When given a set of candidate solutions as input, the searching algorithm will pick one solution from it as the output. A : 2 S → S A: 2^S \rightarrow S \(A(S) = argmin_{s_i \in \underline{S}} T(s_i), \underline{S} \subseteq S\) Note that in the real world, a searching algorithm may pick a suboptimal solution from the solution space. In TensorRT, this suboptimality can arise from at least two sources: Heuristics used during searching: A heuristic may remove candidates before they can be evaluated as part of a complete engine. For example, the builder may filter certain convolution tactics according to a channel-dimension threshold in a certain layer of the input model. If a filtered tactic would have participated in the fastest end-to-end solution, the searching algorithm can no longer discover that optimal solution. A mismatch between local profiling and end-to-end execution: During engine building, kernel candidates may be profiled individually during tactic selection, however, performance is measured across the complete engine when inference. A kernel running in isolation and the same kernel running as part of a larger graph do not share an identical execution environment (for example, the adaptive grid sizing technique used in an NVIDIA Blackwell GPU). Consequently, the sum of individually measured kernel runtimes does not necessarily equal the end-to-end runtime. In the ideal case, the builder algorithm generates a candidate set containing \(s^*\), and the searching algorithm reliably selects it: A ( S ) = s ∗ A(S) = s^* A deep learning compiler can therefore be represented by an algorithm tuple \((A, B)\), where \(B\) generates candidate solutions and \(A\) selects among them. In an actual implementation, however, candidate generation, pruning, profiling, and selection may be tightly coupled. The boundary between \(A\) and \(B\) may therefore not be explicit in the compiler architecture. Let \(B^*\) denote the optimal builder algorithm among the builder algorithm family, and \(A^*\) denote the optimal searching algorithm in the searching algorithm family. The ideal compiler would implement the tuple \((A^*,B^*)\). For any input model, this tuple would generate a candidate set containing the global optimal solution and then reliably discover it: ∀ A , B , ∀ m ∈ M , T ( A ∗ ( B ∗ ( m ) ) ) ≤ T ( A ( B ( m ) ) ) \forall A, B, \forall m \in M, T(A^*(B^*(m))) \leq T(A(B(m))) At the level of the mathematical abstraction, one possible implementation of \(A^*\) is brute-force algorithm—evaluate every solution in the candidate set and select the one with the lowest runtime: \(A^*(S) = argmin_{s_i \in S} T(s_i)\) Though applying the brute-force searching algorithm will not always be acceptable when the build time budget is limited, there could be trade-offs between build time and inference performance. \(A^*\) is used to represent the searching algorithms that will definitely return the optimal solution given any input model. Constructing \(B^*\) is the more fundamental challenge. Even an ideal searching algorithm cannot select a solution that the builder never makes reachable. Rather than expecting to construct \(B^*\) in a single step, it’s possible to progressively approximate it by expanding and improving the build routes available to the compiler. Global Performance Tuner modeling This section models compilation as a sequence of compiler passes, then shows how customizable build routes provide a foundation for accuracy-aware performance tuning. Deep learning compiler modeling Like a traditional compiler, a deep learning compiler can be viewed as a sequence of passes, each of which transforms one IR into another. As previously mentioned, IR has a one-to-one mapping to the final executable binary; thus IR could be thought of as a solution. For this abstraction, let \(f\) represent an IR self-map from the solution space to the solution space: \(f : S \rightarrow S\) \(f(s) = s’\) The builder algorithm of a deep learning compiler can be modeled as a series of passes to convert one solution to another solution: B ( m ) = f k − 1 ( f k − 2 ( . . . ( f 1 ( f 0 ( m ) ) ) ) ) = f k − 1 ∘ f k − 2 ∘ . . . ∘ f 0 ( m ) B(m) = f_{k-1}(f_{k-2}(…(f_1(f_0(m))))) = f_{k-1} \circ f_{k-2} \circ … \circ f_0 (m) B = f k − 1 ∘ f k − 2 ∘ . . . ∘ f 1 ∘ f 0 B = f_{k-1} \circ f_{k-2} \circ … \circ f_1 \circ f_0 The builder algorithm \(B\) is a function composite that looks like a route that the model walks through and gets transformed into a solution space, so \(B\) can also be called a build route. Note the following: Strictly speaking, at least one compiler pass (such as the final code-generation transition) maps from model space \(M\) into executable solution space \(S\). However, compiler passes are not always perfectly decoupled, and an IR can be treated as uniquely identifying the engine produced by the remaining fixed pipeline. Modeling the passes as transformations over a generalized solution-state space therefore provides a useful simplification. Some compiler passes are functionally indispensable while not participating in the performance choices under study. Such performance-irrelevant passes can be treated as identity mapping or omitted from the tunable portion of the route because they do not distinguish one route from another. At first glance, the composition above may appear to imply that one build route generates only one solution (that is, the built engine). In practice, the TensorRT compilation pipeline may consider and filter many potential tactics before producing the final engine. Much of this candidate-generation process remains implicit in the composition because algorithms \(A\) and \(B\) are tightly coupled. The formula describes the selected solution, not every candidate that was considered or discarded along the way. Customizable build route Experience from performance analysis and optimization shows that effective scheduling is model-dependent. Different models can benefit from different choices in individual compiler components, even when they run on the same target GPU. Consequently, the optimal solutions for all models do not necessarily originate from one universal build route. A build route should therefore be customizable, allowing scheduling decisions that adapt to the model and its deployment environment. Such a tunable builder algorithm can be called a customizable build route. For example, consider two models, \(m\) and \(m’\), and a family of available build routes: \(\{B_1, B_2, \ldots, B_n\}\) The two models need not share the same optimal route. Model \(m\) may achieve its best result through \(B_3\), while model \(m’\) may achieve its best result through \(B_1\): \(A^*(B(m)) = \arg\min_{B_i(m)} \{T(B_1(m)), T(B_2(m)), \ldots, T(B_n(m))\} = B_3(m)\) \(A^*(B(m’)) = \arg\min_{B_i(m’)} \{T(B_1(m’)), T(B_2(m’)), \ldots, T(B_n(m’))\} = B_1(m’)\) The Global Performance Tuner begins with the idea of customizable build routes. For each candidate solution, it validates the outputs against the specified accuracy criterion and measures end-to-end inference performance. Among all solutions that meet accuracy requirements, the searching algorithm selects the minimum-runtime feasible solution from the expanded solution set. The following three principles define the framework: Accuracy-aware tuning : Use end-to-end accuracy as a constraint that guides performance tuning. Customizable build route : Make build routes customizable so that scheduling can adapt to each model and deployment environment. Large solution space : Construct a rich feasible solution set, then select the fastest candidate whose numerical difference remains within the specified tolerance. items.raw_text: Edge Computing Scaling NVIDIA TensorRT Performance Optimization Beyond a Single Build Route with the Global Performance Tuner, Part 1 Oct 23, 2026 By Jian Hu and Lin Chai Like Discuss (0) L T F R E AI-Generated Summary NVIDIA TensorRT builds inference engines by making interdependent scheduling decisions across graph transformations, fusion, implementation selection, memory placement, and quantization. A mathematical framework models compilation as a builder algorithm generating candidate solutions and a searching algorithm selecting the fastest feasible one under accuracy constraints. The Global Performance Tuner, released in TensorRT 11.1 , introduces customizable build routes that expand the solution space and validate each candidate against end-to-end accuracy and performance. Three principles guide the tuner: accuracy-aware tuning, customizable build routes, and a large solution space from which the fastest acceptable engine is selected. Next Steps Read the Global Performance Tuner documentation to understand the feature and its configuration options. Read Part 2 of this series for the algorithm and architecture design plus best practices. Powered by NVIDIA Nemotron. AI-generated content may summarize information incompletely. Verify important information. Learn more Deploying a trained neural network involves more than translating each operator into a GPU kernel. It is a compilation problem with many legitimate answers. For example, when NVIDIA TensorRT builds an engine, it makes interdependent decisions about graph-IR transformations, fusion, implementation selection, memory placement, and quantization. This process is called scheduling. Different scheduling choices can preserve model semantics yet produce very different inference performance, making scheduling central to deep learning compiler optimization. No single scheduling strategy is best for every model and deployment environment. A transformation that accelerates one network may slow another. A kernel that is faster in isolation may interact poorly with fusion, tensor layouts, or memory traffic elsewhere in the graph. Aggressive scheduling may improve performance while violating an application’s accuracy requirement. These coupled, model-dependent effects often appear only after the complete engine is built and measured, making the right strategy increasingly difficult to predict. This post is Part 1 of a two-part series that is intended to develop a clearer way of reasoning about performance optimization. It explores questions such as: What makes one compiled engine better than another? Why can individually promising decisions fail end to end? How should accuracy constrain performance optimization? It introduces the Global Performance Tuner , a feature for automatic performance tuning released in TensorRT 11.1 , and explores these questions through an intuitive example and mathematical framework. What challenge does the Global Performance Tuner feature solve? The following analogy illustrates the motivation for building the Global Performance Tuner feature in TensorRT. Imagine a chef with one excellent dish that has pleased three regular customers for years. One likes spice, another sweet-and-sour flavors, and the third extra salt. The chef combines chili, syrup, lemon, and salt in one standard recipe that satisfies all three. One day, a new fourth customer arrives who dislikes spice. Keeping the chili disappoints the newcomer; removing it risks losing the first customer. The root cause of the chef’s dilemma is the method of adding the seasonings does not scale out: the number of interacting exceptions grows with the customer base, and a change for one customer can degrade the meal for another. Figure 1. One fixed recipe does not scale to conflicting customer preferences A scalable approach keeps the base dish but makes the seasonings configurable. The chef records an appropriate combination for each regular customer. For a new customer with unknown preferences, the chef offers free samples with different combinations, rejects unsuitable variations, and keeps the one the customer likes best. Figure 2. Customize the flavor for each customer Mapping this analogy to deep learning compilation, TensorRT is the chef, its shared pipeline the base recipe, tunable compiler configurations the seasonings, and the compiled engine the finished dish. Each ONNX model is a customer. Performance tuning offers samples, and end-to-end performance reflects customer satisfaction. Historically, TensorRT performance optimization has started with internal KPI models. Engineers study these workloads, identify optimizable patterns, and encode their findings as heuristics in the TensorRT default scheduling strategy. Each heuristic captures expert knowledge and allows users to benefit automatically from optimizations discovered on representative models. As models and deployment environments diversify, this approach leads to a scaling problem similar to the one described in the analogy. A heuristic inspired by one internal KPI model joins the shared strategy and may help familiar patterns while causing a regression for an unseen external model. Adding another check or exception may protect that model, but repeating the process makes the scheduling logic increasingly difficult to extend. The problem appears in three related forms: H euristic sprawl: Each new model-specific heuristic introduces another rule whose interactions with existing rules must be understood and maintained. As these rules accumulate, the code becomes unmaintainable, and improvements for one family of models can unintentionally affect another. Performance-accuracy entanglement: Reduced-precision kernels and other aggressive optimizations can improve performance while introducing numerical differences that exceed an application’s acceptable tolerance. Higher-precision choices may reduce that risk but sacrifice performance. Performance and numerical acceptability therefore cannot always be optimized independently. Performance customization: Scheduling choices that work well for one model or GPU may not work well for another. Encoding every successful choice into one universal scheduling strategy makes it difficult to specialize TensorRT efficiently for a continually expanding range of external models, hardware platforms, and application requirements. Tuning provides a scalable complement to heuristic optimization. Mathematical theory for deep learning compiler performance This section develops an abstract mathematical model of deep learning compiler performance. The purpose is to separate two fundamental questions: What executables a compiler can construct for a model How the compiler selects one from those possibilities for optimal performance Concept: Model, model space Let \(m\) represent a model and \(M\) represent the collection of all models under consideration, called the model space: \(m \in M\) Here, a model is an abstract description of the computation to be compiled. Its concrete representation may be an ONNX graph, a network created through the TensorRT API, a PyTorch model, or another frontend representation that fully specifies the model computation. Concept: Solution, solution space Given a model \(m\) as input, a deep learning compiler constructs an executable output for the target hardware, defined as a solution. The same model can generally be compiled into different solutions under different scheduling policies. Let \(s\) represent one such solution, and let \(S\) represent the collection of possible solutions, called the solution space. s ∈ S = { s 0 , s 1 , s 2 , . . . , s n } s \in S = \{s_0, s_1, s_2, …, s_n\} A solution is an abstraction of executable computation on the target hardware. Concretely, a solution may be a TensorRT engine or a cubin of serialized sequence of GPU kernels. More abstractly, it may also be a compiler’s intermediate representation (IR), provided that the representation uniquely determines the final executable under the remaining compilation process. Each solution also defines a function from the model’s input domain to its output codomain: \(s : X \rightarrow Y\) \(s(x) = y\) Here, \((x,y)\) is an input-output pair for the sequence of GPU kernels that implements the neural network. At this level of abstraction, the model describes the intended computation, while a solution describes one particular way of realizing that computation on the target hardware. Principle of determinism Statement: When both a deterministic program and its complete execution environment remain fixed, the program has a fixed underlying run time. This principle serves as a modeling assumption for performance analysis. Under a rigorous interpretation, the environment includes the input data, target device, software stack, GPU frequency, temperature, power state, system load, and other execution conditions that may influence runtime. In practice, not every environmental variable can be controlled perfectly, so repeated runtime measurements exhibit noise. If this disturbance is modeled as independent Gaussian noise, the average of repeated measurements is the maximum-likelihood estimation of the underlying mean run time. Once the execution environment has been fixed at the level required by the abstraction, each solution can be associated with one characteristic runtime. This association enables runtime to be represented as a mathematical function. Concept: Run time function The run time function \(T\) maps each solution to its runtime on a specified target device under a fixed execution environment: T : S → ℝ + T : S \rightarrow \mathbb{R}^+ \(T(s_0) = t_0\) The environment is treated as fixed and is therefore omitted from the notation. Concept: Builder algorithm A builder algorithm (also called a performance scheduler) is a mapping from the model space to the power set of solution space. When given a specific model as input, the builder algorithm will output a solution space with a given accuracy requirement. B : M → 2 S B: M \rightarrow 2^S B ( m ) = { s 1 , s 2 , . . . , s n | max x ∈ X ⁡ ‖ s ( x ) − y ‖ ≤ ϵ } = S B(m) = \{s_1, s_2, …, s_n \mid \max_{x \in X} \norm{ s(x) – y } \leq \epsilon \} = S In the accuracy condition shown above, the input–output pairs \((x, y)\) are treated as reference values, and \(ε\) represents the accuracy tolerance threshold. The reference data, comparison metric, and tolerance are treated as fixed context and are therefore suppressed from the arguments of \(B\). Ideally, the builder algorithm should generate a sufficiently rich set of solutions to contain \(s^*\), the optimal solution: the fastest feasible solution in the modeled solution space. s ∗ ∈ B ( m ) s^* \in B(m) Concept: Searching algorithm A searching algorithm (also called a solver of solution space) is a mapping from the power set of solution space to the solution space. When given a set of candidate solutions as input, the searching algorithm will pick one solution from it as the output. A : 2 S → S A: 2^S \rightarrow S \(A(S) = argmin_{s_i \in \underline{S}} T(s_i), \underline{S} \subseteq S\) Note that in the real world, a searching algorithm may pick a suboptimal solution from the solution space. In TensorRT, this suboptimality can arise from at least two sources: Heuristics used during searching: A heuristic may remove candidates before they can be evaluated as part of a complete engine. For example, the builder may filter certain convolution tactics according to a channel-dimension threshold in a certain layer of the input model. If a filtered tactic would have participated in the fastest end-to-end solution, the searching algorithm can no longer discover that optimal solution. A mismatch between local profiling and end-to-end execution: During engine building, kernel candidates may be profiled individually during tactic selection, however, performance is measured across the complete engine when inference. A kernel running in isolation and the same kernel running as part of a larger graph do not share an identical execution environment (for example, the adaptive grid sizing technique used in an NVIDIA Blackwell GPU). Consequently, the sum of individually measured kernel runtimes does not necessarily equal the end-to-end runtime. In the ideal case, the builder algorithm generates a candidate set containing \(s^*\), and the searching algorithm reliably selects it: A ( S ) = s ∗ A(S) = s^* A deep learning compiler can therefore be represented by an algorithm tuple \((A, B)\), where \(B\) generates candidate solutions and \(A\) selects among them. In an actual implementation, however, candidate generation, pruning, profiling, and selection may be tightly coupled. The boundary between \(A\) and \(B\) may therefore not be explicit in the compiler architecture. Let \(B^*\) denote the optimal builder algorithm among the builder algorithm family, and \(A^*\) denote the optimal searching algorithm in the searching algorithm family. The ideal compiler would implement the tuple \((A^*,B^*)\). For any input model, this tuple would generate a candidate set containing the global optimal solution and then reliably discover it: ∀ A , B , ∀ m ∈ M , T ( A ∗ ( B ∗ ( m ) ) ) ≤ T ( A ( B ( m ) ) ) \forall A, B, \forall m \in M, T(A^*(B^*(m))) \leq T(A(B(m))) At the level of the mathematical abstraction, one possible implementation of \(A^*\) is brute-force algorithm—evaluate every solution in the candidate set and select the one with the lowest runtime: \(A^*(S) = argmin_{s_i \in S} T(s_i)\) Though applying the brute-force searching algorithm will not always be acceptable when the build time budget is limited, there could be trade-offs between build time and inference performance. \(A^*\) is used to represent the searching algorithms that will definitely return the optimal solution given any input model. Constructing \(B^*\) is the more fundamental challenge. Even an ideal searching algorithm cannot select a solution that the builder never makes reachable. Rather than expecting to construct \(B^*\) in a single step, it’s possible to progressively approximate it by expanding and improving the build routes available to the compiler. Global Performance Tuner modeling This section models compilation as a sequence of compiler passes, then shows how customizable build routes provide a foundation for accuracy-aware performance tuning. Deep learning compiler modeling Like a traditional compiler, a deep learning compiler can be viewed as a sequence of passes, each of which transforms one IR into another. As previously mentioned, IR has a one-to-one mapping to the final executable binary; thus IR could be thought of as a solution. For this abstraction, let \(f\) represent an IR self-map from the solution space to the solution space: \(f : S \rightarrow S\) \(f(s) = s’\) The builder algorithm of a deep learning compiler can be modeled as a series of passes to convert one solution to another solution: B ( m ) = f k − 1 ( f k − 2 ( . . . ( f 1 ( f 0 ( m ) ) ) ) ) = f k − 1 ∘ f k − 2 ∘ . . . ∘ f 0 ( m ) B(m) = f_{k-1}(f_{k-2}(…(f_1(f_0(m))))) = f_{k-1} \circ f_{k-2} \circ … \circ f_0 (m) B = f k − 1 ∘ f k − 2 ∘ . . . ∘ f 1 ∘ f 0 B = f_{k-1} \circ f_{k-2} \circ … \circ f_1 \circ f_0 The builder algorithm \(B\) is a function composite that looks like a route that the model walks through and gets transformed into a solution space, so \(B\) can also be called a build route. Note the following: Strictly speaking, at least one compiler pass (such as the final code-generation transition) maps from model space \(M\) into executable solution space \(S\). However, compiler passes are not always perfectly decoupled, and an IR can be treated as uniquely identifying the engine produced by the remaining fixed pipeline. Modeling the passes as transformations over a generalized solution-state space therefore provides a useful simplification. Some compiler passes are functionally indispensable while not participating in the performance choices under study. Such performance-irrelevant passes can be treated as identity mapping or omitted from the tunable portion of the route because they do not distinguish one route from another. At first glance, the composition above may appear to imply that one build route generates only one solution (that is, the built engine). In practice, the TensorRT compilation pipeline may consider and filter many potential tactics before producing the final engine. Much of this candidate-generation process remains implicit in the composition because algorithms \(A\) and \(B\) are tightly coupled. The formula describes the selected solution, not every candidate that was considered or discarded along the way. Customizable build route Experience from performance analysis and optimization shows that effective scheduling is model-dependent. Different models can benefit from different choices in individual compiler components, even when they run on the same target GPU. Consequently, the optimal solutions for all models do not necessarily originate from one universal build route. A build route should therefore be customizable, allowing scheduling decisions that adapt to the model and its deployment environment. Such a tunable builder algorithm can be called a customizable build route. For example, consider two models, \(m\) and \(m’\), and a family of available build routes: \(\{B_1, B_2, \ldots, B_n\}\) The two models need not share the same optimal route. Model \(m\) may achieve its best result through \(B_3\), while model \(m’\) may achieve its best result through \(B_1\): \(A^*(B(m)) = \arg\min_{B_i(m)} \{T(B_1(m)), T(B_2(m)), \ldots, T(B_n(m))\} = B_3(m)\) \(A^*(B(m’)) = \arg\min_{B_i(m’)} \{T(B_1(m’)), T(B_2(m’)), \ldots, T(B_n(m’))\} = B_1(m’)\) The Global Performance Tuner begins with the idea of customizable build routes. For each candidate solution, it validates the outputs against the specified accuracy criterion and measures end-to-end inference performance. Among all solutions that meet accuracy requirements, the searching algorithm selects the minimum-runtime feasible solution from the expanded solution set. The following three principles define the framework: Accuracy-aware tuning : Use end-to-end accuracy as a constraint that guides performance tuning. Customizable build route : Make build routes customizable so that scheduling can adapt to each model and deployment environment. Large solution space : Construct a rich feasible solution set, then select the fastest candidate whose numerical difference remains within the specified tolerance. The mathematical representation of the Global Performance Tuner can be written as: ℬ = { B 1 , B 2 , . . . , B n } \mathcal{B} = \{B_1, B_2, …, B_n\} s ∗ = A ( B 1 ( m ) ∪ B 2 ( m ) ∪ ⋯ ∪ B n ( m ) ) s^* = A(B_1(m) \cup B_2(m) \cup \dots \cup B_n(m)) Learn more To learn more, check out the Global Performance Tuner documentation and read Part 2 of this series, which describes the algorithm and architecture design of the Global Performance Tuner and best practices for using it.
